components.name: torso
components.description: Large faceted torso/body, the dominant horizontally elongated mass centered above the leg set; broad barrel-like cross-section with a deeper chest at the front and a slightly narrowing rump toward the rear. Use a low-resolution loft or hull from several polygonal sections to preserve the angular faceted appearance. No through-openings; the spaces beneath the belly and between legs remain open negative space.

components.name: neck
components.description: Distinct upright neck rising from the front shoulder and blending into the head; substantially narrower than the torso, with a forward-leaning upper profile and faceted tapered cross-sections. Use a short loft or overlapping hull segments rather than a cylindrical neck.

components.name: head
components.description: Elk head projecting forward from the neck, with a tapered wedge-like skull, angular brow and cheek planes, and a narrower muzzle. Keep the head visibly separate in silhouette from the torso and neck while maintaining a continuous animal form. No facial through-openings are required.

components.name: muzzle
components.description: Short forward muzzle/nose extension with a blunt, slightly widened terminal profile and a subtly downturned underside; smaller than the cranium and clearly visible in side silhouette. Preserve the open negative space below the muzzle and above the front-leg region.

components.name: ears
components.description: Two small angular ears mounted high on either side of the head behind the antler bases; each is a thin tapered wedge with a pointed or chamfered tip, splayed slightly outward. The gap between the ears and the antler branches is an intentional visible opening.

components.name: antlers
components.description: Paired broad branching antlers growing from the top of the skull, extending upward and outward above the 150 mm height envelope. Each antler has a thick faceted base, a main rising beam that curves outward, and multiple separated tine branches with tapered pointed ends. Mirror the overall layout across the central sagittal plane with small silhouette variation if needed; retain clear openings between branches and do not fuse neighboring tines into a solid plate. Use segmented lofts or hulls between sampled beam sections, with tapered terminal sections.

components.name: front_legs
components.description: Front leg pair descending from the forward underside of the torso, long and relatively slender with faceted tapering joints; each terminates in a distinct compact hoof angled slightly forward. Keep the two front legs separated by a visible gap and grounded at the same stance plane.

components.name: rear_legs
components.description: Rear leg pair descending from the rump and rear underside, with a characteristic angular or lightly bent hock profile rather than straight cylinders; each narrows toward the ankle and ends in a distinct hoof. Preserve the visible gap between rear legs and the open space between the rear legs and belly.

components.name: hooves
components.description: Four compact faceted hooves, one at the end of each leg, flattened and slightly wedge-shaped with broad ground-contact bottoms. Hooves must remain visibly distinct from the leg shafts and all four lowest contact regions must share the ground plane without adding a support or stand.

components.name: tail
components.description: Short tail at the rear of the torso, projecting rearward and slightly upward as a tapered faceted appendage with a small terminal tuft or blunt point. It is much shorter than the torso and must not be mistaken for an additional leg or antler tine.

relations: The torso is the root structural mass; the neck attaches at its forward upper shoulder, the head and muzzle extend forward from the neck, and the ears and antler bases mount on the upper head/skull.
The elk faces toward -x, with the rear and short tail toward +x; +z is vertical and the two antler/leg sides are arranged across the y axis.

The four legs attach beneath the torso in two separated front/rear pairs. Front legs occupy the forward shoulder region, rear legs occupy the rump region, and all hooves terminate on one common z=0 ground plane.

The antlers are a paired mirrored functional feature centered on the skull and spread primarily in the y direction while rising in +z; branch gaps are intentional negative space, not missing geometry.
The ears sit between the head and antler bases, the muzzle projects ahead of the face, and the tail projects from the rear upper torso with a slight upward angle.

All semantic components are grouped into the single print part elk_body because multiple print parts are not required; the grouping preserves the continuous animal appearance and avoids artificial seams or connectors.

The single-part plan uses ordinary native modeling operations such as low-resolution lofts, hulls, tapered extrusions, and transforms within one Asset hierarchy. No assembly connector is needed because there are no between-part interfaces.
critic_checklist: The final object is a complete static faceted elk with torso, distinct neck, head, muzzle, ears, paired branching antlers, four legs, four hooves, and a short tail all present.

The object uses one scene unit per millimetre, a right-handed Z-up coordinate system, and its final intended-pose dimensions are exactly [141.91845400702914, 141.12070655927337, 150.0] mm within the workflow's measurement tolerance; the longest dimension is 150 mm.
All four hooves contact the same ground plane, the animal remains upright in its natural four-legged stance, and no stand, pedestal, support, unrelated prop, or altered pose is present.
The torso is the dominant mass, the neck is visibly narrower and distinct, and the head and muzzle project forward with recognizable elk proportions rather than forming a generic quadruped blob.
There are exactly four visually identifiable legs and four visually identifiable hooves; front and rear leg pairs remain separated by open negative space under the belly and between adjacent legs.
The rear legs retain an angular hock-like bend, while the front legs descend from the chest with a mostly straight tapered profile; no leg merges into a neighboring leg or hoof.
The antlers extend above the head and are broad, asymmetric-looking in silhouette only where appropriate, with two substantial main beams and multiple clearly separated branching tines on each side.
Antler branches remain connected to the skull through substantial bases, but adjacent tines do not collapse into a solid sheet; visible openings between the main beam and branches are preserved.
The ears, tail, muzzle, and hooves remain visible in the primary reference view and are not swallowed by the torso, neck, antler bases, or ground plane.

The silhouette remains faceted and low-poly: broad planar transitions and angular section changes are intentional, with no unrelated smooth decorative geometry or excessive subdivision that destroys the reference appearance.
The tail is short, rearward-directed, and clearly distinct from the rear legs; it does not extend beyond the intended overall length envelope.

The single planned print part contains every semantic component, so no connector or assembly interface is required; the native FixedAssembly API is used with the torso-rooted print part and no manual second-part placement.
The assembled scene contains no extra geometry after assembly, and the visible result is the complete use-pose object rather than an exploded or supported presentation.
